query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy previously showed limited amorphous retention and a complicated thermal response. Earlier thermal studies of Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P alloys found that rapid quenching could produce amorphous material, but that its stability was limited during subsequent heating. The design challenge is therefore to obtain robust glass formation across relevant cooling conditions without sacrificing stability during reheating. What single intervention could improve amorphous retention and thermal stability during solidification and thermal analysis? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the reported behavior of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the cooling-rate and reheating conditions under which it should or should not succeed, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A sub-Tg relaxation anneal immediately after rapid quenching will improve amorphous retention and thermal stability in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
generation.material_initial_state: Molten Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 rapidly quenched to form an as-quenched amorphous-like structure.
generation.intervention: Hold the alloy at approximately 50 K below its glass transition temperature for 10–15 minutes in an inert environment immediately after rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: This sub-Tg anneal is predicted to be effective at moderate cooling rates (tens to thousands of K/s) and subsequent reheating up to near Tg, but may lose effectiveness if exposed to very slow cooling or temperatures significantly above Tg.
generation.structural_mediator: Relief of internal stresses and reduction of excess free volume in the as-quenched amorphous structure.
generation.mechanism: By relaxing internal strains and lowering the enthalpy state below Tg, the driving force for devitrification is reduced, thereby increasing the onset temperature of crystallization on reheating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to unannealed material, samples receiving the sub-Tg relaxation anneal will show a higher crystallization onset temperature, reduced enthalpy of crystallization, and improved retention of the amorphous phase during thermal analysis.
generation.baseline: Unannealed Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits limited amorphous retention and complex thermal behavior, quickly undergoing devitrification under modest reheating.
generation.boundary: Efficacy of sub-Tg annealing depends on controlling the post-quench temperature precisely. Extremely high reheating temperatures or very slow cooling rates may surpass the range where relaxation can suppress devitrification.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimum relaxation temperature and dwell time for this alloy are not established and may vary depending on the purity, sample geometry, and thermal history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 specimens quenched at a known rate to achieve a similar initial glass fraction; then subject half of the specimens to the proposed sub-Tg anneal. Apply differential scanning calorimetry at various heating rates and compare devitrification onsets, enthalpy changes, and final microstructures between annealed and non-annealed samples.
measurements: X-ray diffraction or electron diffraction patterns to confirm amorphous vs. crystalline content
Microscopic analysis before and after heat treatment to characterize microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sub-Tg-annealed samples do not show an increased crystallization onset temperature or lowered enthalpy of crystallization compared to unannealed references, or if they devitrify at similar or lower temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. Pronounced thermal effects were observed at T3 = 1291 K and T4 = 1206 K during slow cooling on a copper plate (52 K/s), and at T3 = 977 K and T4 = 960 K during rapid cooling following a brief electric arc pulse (3018 K/s). This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. These results highlight the critical importance of controlling cooling rates and alloy composition to optimize phase stability and microstructure. cited_evidence.text: As shown in the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurement in Figure 4D, the crystallization of the amorphous particles is an exothermic process and begins at approximately 375 °C, which is exactly the same temperature where the rapid decrease of the FWHM in Figure 4C starts, and the required thermal energy kBT is achieved to overcome the activation energy. Note that for the determination of the plot in Figure 4C, more temperature steps were considered than those shown in Figure 4B. However, for clarity reasons, the full data set of 94 SAED patterns is not shown and can be found in the Supporting Information File 2 as a video file. The observation of amorphous particles transforming into a crystalline phase validates that the amorphous phase is metastable and forms under kinetic control, whereas the crystalline structure is the thermodynamically favored one [], and thermodynamic control is dominant when activation energy barriers are overcome by heating.

decision.trend: Earlier thermal studies on Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P alloys, as well as on the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 high-entropy alloy itself, reveal a recurring pattern: rapid quenching from the melt can yield an amorphous phase, but that phase tends to devitrify upon reheating. Subsequent work on Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 (PMC11642357) established that faster cooling rates more readily produce an amorphous microstructure, yet stability during thermal analysis remains insufficient. Despite proven glass-forming ability under extreme quench, controlling the devitrification pathway and achieving robust thermal stability have not been fully resolved.
decision.unsolved: The open question is how to retain an amorphous structure over a practical range of cooling rates and to preserve it during later thermal exposures without resorting to new alloying additions.
decision.lever: A sub-Tg relaxation anneal immediately after rapid quenching, for example holding the initially amorphous alloy ~50 K below Tg for short (e.g., 10–15 min) durations in an inert environment. This mild heat treatment aims to reduce free volume and homogenize local stress states before the alloy is fully cooled, lowering the driving force for devitrification upon subsequent heating.
decision.why: The literature (PMC11642357) shows that very high cooling rates can achieve full or mostly amorphous structures, but such glasses are metastable and transform readily upon reheating. A controlled relaxation step at sub-Tg can relieve internal stresses and redistribute structural inhomogeneities, thereby slowing or preventing devitrification even under moderate reheating conditions. Prior evidence on other metallic glasses supports that sub-Tg annealing can stabilize the amorphous network by reducing excess enthalpy. This hypothesis can be falsified if the sub-Tg-annealed alloy still crystallizes at the same or lower threshold temperature than the unannealed material when subjected to differential scanning calorimetry, indicating insufficient relaxation to arrest devitrification.
